transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Ever since my wife brought up separating, I feel like I’m not coping with it well at all and it’s throwing off how I function at home and at work. It has just been incredibly difficult to keep things together lately.
When did your wife first bring up separating, and did these difficulties start within about 3 months of that? Have they been getting better, worse, or staying about the same since then?

My wife brought up the separation about a month ago, and these difficulties started almost immediately—within just a few days of that conversation. Since then, it’s been pretty constant and hasn't really gotten any better over this past month.
How much is this affecting your day-to-day life—for example, are you having trouble doing your job, taking care of things at home, or keeping up with relationships because of this?

It's significantly affecting both my work and home life. At work, I've missed key follow-up details, which has caused a couple of important deals to stall. At home, I've been so distracted and unreliable that my wife has had to take over most of the logistics with our kids, and I've found myself snapping at them over little things.

Compared with what most people might feel during a separation, does your reaction feel much more intense than expected for the situation? Also, is this mainly related to the separation rather than the death of someone close to you?

Yes, my reaction feels completely overwhelming and far more intense than how I'd expect to handle a tough situation, and it's really throwing off my ability to function. This is entirely triggered by my wife bringing up the separation, and it has nothing to do with the death of a loved one.

Before your wife brought up separating, were you already having significant depression, anxiety, panic attacks, or other mental health symptoms? Or did all of this begin only after the separation was brought up?

All of this started only after my wife brought up the separation. Before that conversation, I wasn't having any of these mental health struggles or any trouble keeping things together. It was only after she suggested living apart that everything began to unravel.

The reaction is not related to bereavement, and the patient reports no prior depression, anxiety, panic, or other mental health symptoms before the stressor, supporting adjustment disorder.
